title: Al-Hamid, the Praiseworthy
tomorrow: you can't count His gifts. so what does the Counter count?

lines: AFTER A SNEEZE, AFTER A MEAL.
cards: Some words are less said than breathed. In some Muslim homes one comes back all day: after a sneeze, after a meal, after a long sip of cold water on a hot afternoon.
And sometimes right after a wince, which is the one that puzzles people. Alhamdulillah. Praise belongs to God.
From outside, it can sound like "it's fine, don't worry about me." It isn't that.

teach.h: PRAISE BE TO ALLAH, LORD OF THE WORLDS.
teach.b: Today's Name is Al-Hamid, the Praiseworthy. In the Qur'an's first surah, right after the name of God, comes this, in Pickthall's words: "Praise be to Allah, Lord of the Worlds."

teach.h: PRAISED EVEN IF ALL ARE THANKLESS.
teach.b: And in Surah Ibrahim, Moses tells his people something sharp: "Though ye and all who are in the earth prove thankless, lo! Allah verily is Absolute, Owner of Praise." Notice what that means.
Al-Hamid isn't praiseworthy because people praise Him. If everyone on earth went quiet, the praise would still be His. So alhamdulillah isn't a report on how your day went.

teach.h: A SENTENCE ABOUT GOD, NOT YOUR DAY.
teach.b: It's a sentence about God, and that's why it can be said with tears on your face. The Prophet, peace be upon him, kept two versions, as hadith reports describe.
When something pleased him, he praised the One by whose grace good things are completed.
When something hurt, he said alhamdulillah 'ala kulli hal: praise to Allah in every state.
Here's one to tell a friend: there's even an exchange for a sneeze. The one who sneezes says alhamdulillah, and the one who hears answers, may Allah have mercy on you.
A sound the body makes by accident, turned into praise and a blessing in two lines.

how: Muslims say alhamdulillah after meals, after sneezing, on good news and in hardship ('alhamdulillah 'ala kulli hal'), and it opens al-Fatiha, recited in the daily prayers.

o: the Praiseworthy, worthy in every state
the Thankful, who rewards every thanks
the Glorious, praised only in heaven

games.q: where the praise shows up — tap the pairs.
p: Praise be to Allah, Lord of the Worlds
Owner of Praise, even if all are thankless

s: saying alhamdulillah while hurting means pretending it doesn't hurt
alhamdulillah 'ala kulli hal: praise in every state. it's a sentence about God, not a rating of your pain.
the Qur'an's first surah praises Allah as Lord of the Worlds
"Praise be to Allah, Lord of the Worlds."
Al-Hamid is praiseworthy because people praise Him
Moses: even if all on earth prove thankless, Allah is Owner of Praise.

games.q: your teammate misses the last shot and the season's over. in the locker room he says 'alhamdulillah.' someone laughs: 'for WHAT?' what's the most accurate answer?
o: it's sarcasm, like saying 'great, just great.'
it's praise for God, and that doesn't depend on the score.
he's just relieved the season is finally done.
games.why: Al-Hamid is praiseworthy whatever the outcome; Moses says even if all on earth are thankless. the praise is about God, not the scoreboard.

practice: If there's water near you, pour a glass and hold it a moment, feeling the cold through the glass. Drink it slowly, in three sips, and after the last one say alhamdulillah, out loud or under your breath.
Then sit with the taste fading and the word still there.

wordCard.voice: Al-Hamid. The Praiseworthy: praised in Himself, even in a world gone quiet, so the praise fits every state.

orig.note: Arabic: the Praiseworthy. it shares a root with hamd, the praise in alhamdulillah.

carryVoice: Keep it on the tongue: praised, in the good news and the hard news alike. Until tomorrow.
